The adjacent construction q(x,t) = q̃(x − ūt) describes profiles translated with unchanged shape (printed page 1, (1.3)). Although the introduction says 'any function', the explanatory source qualifies classical differential reasoning by sufficient smoothness and explicitly distinguishes discontinuous integral solutions from classical PDE solutions (printed pages 4–5 and 17–18). The selected statement specifies no positivity constraint on q or ū and no initial or boundary data; later domain and boundary examples are separate problem specifications (printed pages 1 and 18).

The scalar coefficient is real for the stated scalar hyperbolicity claim (printed page 1, paragraph beginning 'The simplest case').

A classical differential interpretation requires the relevant partial derivatives; the surrounding source assumes sufficient smoothness when deriving differential conservation laws, and Chapter 2 explicitly describes smooth translated profiles (printed pages 4–5, section 1.1.2; printed pages 17–18, derivation and (2.13)).

The initial real-product domain is stated for the introductory system, whereas the transport paragraph does not separately specify pipe endpoints or a time interval (printed page 1, paragraph after (1.1) and paragraph introducing (1.2)).

Initial and boundary conditions belong to subsequent problem specifications, with both infinite and finite pipe cases discussed; they are not supplied as hypotheses of equation (1.2) on the selected page (printed page 1, (1.2); printed page 18, initial and boundary condition discussion).

Chapter 2 provides explanatory context for equation (1.2), including its derivation and regularity qualifications; its separate general-solution and initial-boundary-value statements are not independent selected results (locator source scope; printed pages 15–18).
